entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Columbia University, founded as King's College in 1754 in New York City by royal charter of King George II, is America's fifth-oldest institution of higher education and one of the world's leading research universities. Columbia has produced an extraordinary number of influential figures in American public life — 10 US presidents' alumni (including Eisenhower as president), 89 Nobel laureates among faculty, staff, and students, and major contributions to the Manhattan Project, television, and American constitutional development.

King's College was founded to serve the colonial intellectual elite of New York; after the American Revolution it was renamed Columbia College (1784) reflecting American independence from British monarchy. Columbia established the first American law school (1858), first American school of journalism (1912 — now granting the Pulitzer Prizes), and was the site of Manhattan Project uranium research under Enrico Fermi (1942). The 1968 student protests at Columbia — against the Vietnam War and university construction on a community park — became defining symbols of the era's campus radicalism.

Columbia's Morningside Heights campus in upper Manhattan, designed by McKim, Mead & White in Beaux-Arts style, is one of America's finest university campuses. The university's location in New York — the world's media, finance, and culture capital — gives it unique proximity to institutions in every field. Columbia's graduate programs in law, business (CBS), journalism, and international affairs (SIPA) are consistently ranked among the world's best.
